title: Techies Still Rule H-1B Banking Hires as $100K Fee Reshapes Sponsorship
excerpt: Analysis of 17,500 filings shows engineers win nearly half of bank H-1Bs while front-office hires top $300k — as a new $100,000 application fee changes the maths.
body:
• eFinancialCareers analysed 17,500+ H-1B salary filings at banks over two years to map which roles actually get sponsored — and what they pay.
  • Technology staff account for just under half of H-1B filings at the five biggest US banks; front-office bankers and traders are next, earning $180k on average with many above $300k.
  • Quants, risk and compliance hires are also common; hedge funds and prop traders pay H-1B engineers $230k-$300k on average.
  • The data lands as a new $100,000 fee per H-1B application reshapes the economics of sponsorship — hitting low-paid analyst pipelines hardest.

For all the political noise around the H-1B visa, banks still run on it — and new data shows exactly who gets sponsored and what they earn. eFinancialCareers has analysed more than 17,500 salary listings from the H-1B salary database covering the two years to July 31, 2026, mapping the roles most likely to win bank sponsorship.

The headline finding: across the five biggest US banks, just under half of all H-1B filings are confirmed to be for engineers or other technology staff. Technology remains the surest route to a sponsored banking job.

Where the money is

The next most common category, separated by a wide margin, is front-office staff — bankers, traders and relationship managers. These are also the highest earners: front-office H-1Bs average $180,000 in salary, with many earning $300,000 or more.

Quants, risk and compliance staff are other popular H-1B categories. Roughly 20% of filings did not declare any function and listed only seniority, according to the analysis.

The pay data at elite firms is striking. At hedge fund Two Sigma, the average H-1B software engineer filed in 2025 earned $231,000 in salary alone, with the highest offer at $306,000. Jane Street paid its H-1B software engineers $300,000 on average. Among banks, JPMorgan — the biggest H-1B employer in banking — spreads its highest-paid H-1Bs across divisions, while UBS's top H-1B earner, a managing director in family-office coverage, earned $500,000. Citi's highest-paid H-1B holder in 2025 was a New York product manager on $612,000.

The $100,000 question

The data arrives as the economics of sponsorship shift. A recent executive order mandates a one-time $100,000 fee for each new H-1B application — a sum that changes the calculus most for low-paid, high-volume pipelines.

Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan together filed at least 3,933 H-1B applications in 2025, paying holders $145,000 on average. But the distribution matters: Goldman has more than 100 H-1Bs earning under $100,000 — mostly entry-level analysts — while JPMorgan has just four. A proposed wage-based allocation system could further squeeze graduate-level opportunities.

What this means for Indian aspirants

Indians remain the largest beneficiaries of the H-1B programme, and the data carries a clear message: technology skills are still the most reliable ticket, while front-office roles pay the most but are harder to land. With the $100,000 fee raising the bar, banks are likely to concentrate sponsorship on roles where the salary justifies the cost — favouring experienced engineers, quants and revenue-generating front-office hires over entry-level analysts.

For students and early-career professionals, the practical takeaway is to target employers with a demonstrated history of sponsorship in your exact role — public LCA disclosure data shows the job title, wage level and worksite of every certified filing — and to treat the H-1B less as a lottery ticket and more as a labour-market transaction where skills and salary set the odds.
